behavior_items: The reproducer defines a C-interoperable derived type `t` using `type, bind(c) :: t` with one `integer(c_int)` component. This makes `t` a concrete interoperable Fortran type suitable for `bind(c)` procedure interfaces.

The external interface in `z1.f90` declares `function f(x) bind(c) result(z)` with dummy argument `type(t) :: x(:)`. An assumed-shape array dummy in a `bind(c)` interface is represented through C descriptor machinery rather than plain by-reference scalar passing, so lowering the call requires descriptor conversion logic.

The actual argument at the call site is `y`, declared as `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)`. This is an unlimited polymorphic allocatable array descriptor, meaning its runtime representation carries dynamic type information and Fortran descriptor metadata rather than matching the static nonpolymorphic `type(t)` array dummy directly.

The statement `n = f(y)` forces the front end to resolve and lower a procedure call where the actual argument is an unlimited polymorphic allocatable array and the formal argument is a nonpolymorphic interoperable assumed-shape array. This combination is the key stress case of the reproducer.

Even though this argument association is semantically dubious and should at most lead to a normal compile-time diagnostic about type/rank/interoperability mismatch, the compiler instead proceeds into code generation for descriptor conversion.

During lowering of the procedure call, GCC Fortran reaches `gfc_conv_procedure_call`, which invokes `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc`. That routine is responsible for converting a gfortran internal descriptor into a CFI descriptor suitable for a `bind(c)` array argument.

The ICE location shows that the compiler assumes it can construct a CFI descriptor from the actual argument descriptor for this call. However, the actual is unlimited polymorphic (`class(*)`) and allocatable, while the formal expects a specific interoperable element type `t`. The conversion path does not safely handle that mismatch.

Because the crash occurs in translation (`trans-expr.cc`) rather than parsing or semantic resolution, the bug is not merely rejection of invalid source; it is a missing guard or incorrect assumption in the lowering path that allows an unsupported actual/formal descriptor combination to reach ICE-prone code.

The reproducer is minimal because nothing about allocation status or runtime execution matters: the program is only compiled with `-c`. The failure is purely compile-time and is triggered solely by the static shape/type/interface combination at the call expression.

The regression note 'since r9' indicates older compilers such as gfortran 8 compile this testcase without crashing. Therefore, some change introduced after GCC 8 caused the front end to route this call through newer descriptor-conversion code without preserving the necessary validity checks.

The same pattern is shown in two source forms: `z1.f90` uses an explicit interface block for an external `bind(c)` function, while `z2.f90` defines the `bind(c)` function internally in a `contains` section. Both forms exercise the same essential behavior: passing `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)` to a `bind(c)` dummy `type(t) :: x(:)`.

The important language features interacting here are: `iso_c_binding`, `bind(c)` procedure semantics, assumed-shape array dummies, C descriptor lowering, unlimited polymorphism via `class(*)`, and allocatable array descriptors. The bug is exposed specifically where these features intersect.

The stack trace confirms the path: expression lowering of `f(y)` inside assignment, then procedure-call lowering, then descriptor conversion. This strongly suggests the compiler has already accepted enough of the call to build a backend representation and crashes when trying to encode the actual argument as a C interoperable descriptor.

A robust compiler behavior for this testcase would be either: reject the call during semantic checking because an unlimited polymorphic allocatable array cannot match `type(t) :: x(:)` in this `bind(c)` context, or otherwise lower it safely if valid. Crashing indicates a front-end correctness bug rather than a user-code runtime issue.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer exercises GCC Fortran's lowering of a `bind(c)` procedure call with an assumed-shape array dummy of interoperable derived type `t`, but passes an actual argument of type `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)`. That actual/formal combination drives the compiler into descriptor conversion code for C interoperability. Instead of issuing a normal type/interoperability mismatch diagnostic or handling the case safely, newer GCC versions reach `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc` and ICE while attempting to convert the unlimited-polymorphic Fortran descriptor into a CFI descriptor expected for the `bind(c)` dummy. The bug is therefore a regression in front-end call lowering and descriptor conversion for mismatched polymorphic array arguments in C-interoperable procedure interfaces.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a Fortran front-end regression in the BIND(C) array-descriptor lowering path. The testcase combines: (1) a C-interoperable procedure interface, (2) an assumed-shape array dummy that requires CFI descriptor construction, and (3) an actual argument that is unlimited polymorphic and allocatable (`class(*)`). The compiler accepts enough of this mismatched call to enter code generation, then crashes in `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc` while converting the gfortran descriptor to a C descriptor. This indicates the failure is not in parsing but in missing semantic rejection, missing validity checks, or wrong assumptions in descriptor conversion/lowering for polymorphic actual arguments passed to nonpolymorphic interoperable dummies. Since the regression started after GCC 8 and the ICE occurs specifically in `gfc_conv_procedure_call` -> `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc`, the most likely defect is newly introduced CFI-descriptor conversion logic that does not guard against unsupported `class(*)`/allocatable descriptors or type incompatibility before dereferencing or encoding element-type metadata.
possible_causes: Missing front-end semantic check for passing `class(*), allocatable` assumed-rank/assumed-shape descriptor actuals to a nonpolymorphic `type(t) :: x(:)` BIND(C) dummy, allowing invalid argument association to reach lowering.
`gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc` assumes the actual descriptor has a concrete interoperable element type and fails when the actual is unlimited polymorphic, causing ICE instead of graceful rejection.

Descriptor-conversion code for BIND(C) array arguments does not handle polymorphic/allocatable descriptor variants and likely accesses absent or incompatible type metadata when building the CFI descriptor.

Regression in `gfc_conv_procedure_call` argument lowering: it routes mismatched polymorphic array actuals through the CFI conversion path without first checking type compatibility and C interoperability constraints.

Incorrect assumption that any array descriptor actual can be converted to a CFI descriptor for an interoperable dummy, ignoring that `class(*)` descriptors carry dynamic type information not representable as the required static `type(t)` element descriptor.
Failure to reject or specially handle unlimited polymorphic actual arguments in C interoperability code paths introduced around r9, especially for assumed-shape BIND(C) dummies.

Possible missing null/variant check in trans-expr descriptor handling at or near `fortran/trans-expr.cc:5647`, where code may expect a declared derived-type descriptor layout but receives a CLASS(*) descriptor layout instead.
evidence: ICE site is `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc`, which is specifically the descriptor conversion routine used for BIND(C) array argument lowering.
Stack trace shows `gfc_conv_procedure_call` -> `gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc`, confirming the crash happens during procedure-call lowering, not parsing or later optimization.
Formal dummy is `type(t) :: x(:)` in a `bind(c)` function, a case that requires CFI descriptor machinery for assumed-shape arrays.
Actual argument is `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)`, an unlimited polymorphic descriptor with runtime type metadata, not a concrete nonpolymorphic interoperable `type(t)` array.
Behavior summary explicitly notes the call is semantically dubious and should at worst receive a normal compile-time diagnostic, but instead enters code generation and ICEs.
The failure reproduces in both explicit-interface and internal-procedure forms, showing the trigger is the actual/formal descriptor combination rather than one specific name-resolution path.
The bug is a regression since r9; gfortran 8 compiles the testcase without crashing, implicating newer descriptor-conversion/lowering changes rather than long-standing parser behavior.
Compilation uses `-c` only, so runtime allocation status is irrelevant; the crash is purely due to static lowering logic for this argument association.

The testcase intersects `iso_c_binding`, BIND(C), assumed-shape arrays, unlimited polymorphism, and allocatable descriptors—exactly the feature combination most likely to stress unchecked descriptor-conversion assumptions.

selected_files.reason: The ICE is reported directly in gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc at fortran/trans-expr.cc:5647, reached from gfc_conv_procedure_call during lowering of the BIND(C) call. This file contains the descriptor-conversion and procedure-call translation logic most directly implicated by the crash, and the bug description strongly suggests a missing guard or incorrect assumption for CLASS(*) allocatable descriptors converted to CFI descriptors.

A likely upstream cause is failed semantic rejection: the compiler appears to accept an invalid or unsupported actual/formal association long enough to reach lowering. resolve.cc is the main semantic checking and procedure argument resolution file, so it is a strong candidate for a missing compatibility/interoperability check for passing class(*), allocatable arrays to nonpolymorphic type(t) BIND(C) assumed-shape dummies.

The testcase hinges on explicit/internal procedure interface handling for a BIND(C) function with assumed-shape dummy arguments. If interface checking failed to diagnose the mismatch between the unlimited polymorphic actual and the concrete interoperable dummy, interface.cc is a plausible source of the bug in argument compatibility or interface validation logic.

The problematic actual argument is unlimited polymorphic class(*), allocatable :: y(:). class.cc implements Fortran polymorphism machinery and descriptor/class-container handling, making it a plausible place for incorrect metadata assumptions or missing restrictions that later allow an incompatible CLASS(*) descriptor to flow into C interoperability lowering.

CFI descriptor construction depends on backend type metadata for interoperable and polymorphic entities. While less directly implicated than trans-expr.cc, trans-types.cc is a reasonable suspect if the regression involves incorrect type/descriptor representation assumptions for CLASS(*) versus concrete BIND(C) derived-type arrays.

related_methods.reason: This is the exact ICE site named in the bug report. Its documented role is to bridge gfortran descriptors to ISO_Fortran_binding CFI descriptors, which matches the failing BIND(C) assumed-shape argument lowering. The reproducer passes an unlimited polymorphic allocatable descriptor where a concrete interoperable type descriptor is expected, so missing type/variant guards or wrong assumptions here are the most direct cause.

The stack trace shows this caller directly invoking the crashing conversion routine during lowering of f(y). As the main procedure-call lowering routine, it is a prime place for missing compatibility checks before routing a CLASS(*) allocatable array actual into the CFI-descriptor conversion path for a nonpolymorphic BIND(C) dummy.

This is the central resolver for function calls like `f(y)`. The reproducer fails because an invalid or unsupported actual/formal association survives resolution and reaches lowering. This method is the most suspicious place in resolve.cc for missing checks on argument compatibility, especially for `bind(c)` procedures with assumed-shape dummies and unlimited polymorphic actual arguments.

The bug hinges on the actual argument `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)` being accepted far enough to reach descriptor conversion. This method resolves actual arguments and is a likely place where rank/type/polymorphism properties of the actual descriptor should be validated or propagated correctly before later procedure-interface checks.

Most suspicious because it is the core formal-vs-actual argument compatibility checker. The reproducer hinges on an invalid or unsupported association between actual `class(*), allocatable :: y(:)` and formal `type(t) :: x(:)` in a `bind(c)` interface. If this routine fails to reject unlimited polymorphic/allocatable actuals for a nonpolymorphic interoperable dummy, the bad call can incorrectly survive semantics and later ICE in descriptor lowering.

This method performs whole actual/formal argument-list compatibility checking and sorting, and is a likely place where mismatched arguments are still accepted as usable. Since the crash occurs only after the call has been considered valid enough to lower, a bug here could let the problematic `class(*)` array actual pass through without enforcing the needed type/rank/interoperability restrictions for the `bind(c)` assumed-shape dummy.

Most suspicious because the ICE is triggered by an unlimited polymorphic allocatable array actual (`class(*)`) being lowered as a BIND(C) descriptor. This method builds the internal CLASS container representation, including special handling for unlimited polymorphic entities (`_data`, `_vptr`, `_len`). A bug here could leave class(*) symbols with incomplete or inconsistent metadata that later descriptor-conversion code wrongly assumes is concrete and interoperable.

Unlimited polymorphism relies on intrinsic vtabs, and the testcase uses `class(*)`, whose dynamic type information must be represented through that machinery. If intrinsic vtab construction for class(*) or related metadata is wrong or missing for arrays/allocatables, later lowering to a CFI descriptor could mis-handle the actual argument and ICE instead of rejecting it cleanly.

Most suspicious because the ICE happens while lowering a BIND(C) assumed-shape argument through CFI descriptor conversion. This method explicitly builds/returns the CFI type information, so a wrong assumption about the actual descriptor's element type or unsupported CLASS(*)/allocatable cases could directly feed the crashing path in gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc.

The formal dummy element type is a BIND(C) derived type t, while the actual is unlimited polymorphic. Any bug in constructing or reusing backend type nodes for derived types, especially interoperable ones, could cause later descriptor-conversion code to believe it has a concrete interoperable element layout when it does not.

Very unlikely to be related, but this file only contains Darwin Fortran stubs and this method is one of the only selectable candidates. The reported ICE is in the Fortran front end descriptor-conversion path (gfc_conv_gfc_desc_to_cfi_desc in trans-expr.cc), not Objective-C include registration; this stub should not affect BIND(C) argument lowering.

Also very unlikely. It is a Darwin-specific no-op stub for framework/include registration, whereas the bug concerns semantic/lowering handling of polymorphic Fortran descriptors in BIND(C) calls. Included only because the instruction restricts selection to this methods list and there are no plausibly relevant methods here.

Most suspicious only in a relative sense: it is one of the few broad target-initialization routines that can affect front-end/driver behavior globally, but the reported ICE is in Fortran descriptor lowering (trans-expr.cc), not Darwin target code. If this file were implicated at all, an option-setup hook would be the likeliest place for indirect misconfiguration.

This routine computes and caches symbol properties affecting Mach-O code generation. While unrelated to the reported Fortran ICE, it is a central classification function in this file and thus more plausible than narrow section emitters if an incorrect target-side symbol/property assumption somehow interacted with lowering.

Most suspicious only by process of elimination within this file: it is the main driver setup routine and coordinates target/option initialization, so if any Darwin-driver logic could indirectly mis-handle compilation setup it would be here. However, the reported ICE is in the Fortran front end's trans-expr descriptor-conversion path, so this is a very weak match.
